atoms.title: The nuclear atom
atoms.summary: An atom is a tiny dense positive nucleus of protons and neutrons surrounded by a diffuse cloud of electrons.

depths.eli5: Everything around you is made of atoms — unimaginably tiny building blocks. Each atom has a heavy clump at its very center called the nucleus, and a cloud of much lighter specks called electrons whizzing around it. Picture a marble (the nucleus) sitting in the middle of a whole stadium, with a fuzzy swarm of tiny electrons filling all the rest of the empty space. Almost all the weight is in that central marble.
depths.core: An atom is the smallest unit of an element (a pure substance like carbon or oxygen). It is built from three kinds of particle. Protons carry a positive (+1) electric charge; neutrons carry no charge (0); electrons carry a negative (−1) charge. Protons and neutrons are packed tightly together in the central nucleus, which holds nearly all the atom's mass. Electrons occupy the much larger surrounding volume. A famous 1911 experiment by Ernest Rutherford (firing particles at thin gold foil and watching a few bounce straight back) revealed that the positive charge and mass are concentrated in a nucleus about ten-thousand times smaller than the whole atom. The number of protons — called the atomic number, written Z — defines which element you have. Neutrons add mass and tune how stable the nucleus is. Electrons are the part that does the actual chemistry.
depths.deep: Chemistry is almost entirely the behavior of the outermost electrons sitting in the electric field of the nucleus. In ordinary chemical reactions the nucleus is essentially a spectator — it never changes; only electrons are rearranged. The nucleus matters only through its charge Z, which sets how tightly the electrons are held. (Nuclear reactions, where the nucleus itself changes, are a separate subject from chemistry.)

quiz.prompt: Which subatomic particle determines what element an atom is?
quiz.answer: The proton — the number of protons (atomic number Z) defines the element.

quiz.prompt: An atom has 6 protons, 8 neutrons, and 6 electrons. What is it, and is it charged?
quiz.answer: Carbon (Z=6), specifically carbon-14 (mass number 14); equal protons and electrons mean it is neutral.

atoms.title: Quantum numbers and orbitals
atoms.summary: Each electron is labeled by four quantum numbers that name its orbital and spin, and no two electrons in an atom share all four.

depths.eli5: Electrons don't sit still in fixed dots — physics describes each one by a set of four 'address' numbers that say roughly where it lives and how it spins. A strict rule says no two electrons in the same atom can have the exact same four-part address. That rule is why electrons stack up in layers instead of all piling into one spot.
depths.core: In modern physics an electron bound to a nucleus can only exist in certain allowed states, each one labeled by four 'quantum numbers' — fixed numbers that act like an address. (1) n, the principal quantum number (1, 2, 3, …), sets the electron's energy and roughly its distance from the nucleus. (2) ℓ sets the shape of the region the electron occupies; these shapes are named with letters s, p, d, f. A specific region of space an electron occupies is called an orbital. (3) m_ℓ sets the orientation of that shape in space. (4) m_s, the spin (always +½ or −½), is an intrinsic property of the electron, loosely picturable as which way it 'spins'. The Pauli exclusion principle states that no two electrons in one atom may have all four numbers identical — which is exactly why each orbital can hold at most two electrons (and only if their spins differ).
depths.deep: The allowed shapes (the ℓ values) come from the angular part of the solution to the Schrödinger equation — the master equation of quantum mechanics — and are mathematically the spherical harmonics; the radial part (linked to n) fixes the energy. Pauli exclusion is not an extra force pushing electrons apart but a deep consequence of electrons being identical 'fermions': the combined wavefunction describing two of them must flip sign if you swap them, which mathematically forbids them sharing an identical state.

atoms.title: Electron configuration
atoms.summary: Ground-state electrons fill orbitals from lowest energy up, one spin-paired pair at a time, following Aufbau, Hund, and Pauli.

depths.eli5: Think of an atom's orbitals (the regions electrons live in) as seats in a theater priced by how close they are to the front. Electrons fill the cheapest seats first. When several seats cost the same, electrons spread out — one to each — before any seat is shared. And no two ever share an identical seat. Doing this for an atom's electrons gives you its 'electron configuration', a shorthand for where all its electrons sit.
depths.core: An electron configuration lists which orbitals an atom's electrons occupy in its lowest-energy (ground) state. You build it with three rules. The Aufbau principle ('building-up'): add electrons one at a time to the lowest-energy orbital still available. Hund's rule: when several orbitals have the same energy (called 'degenerate'), put one electron in each, all spinning the same way, before doubling any up — this keeps electrons apart and lowers repulsion. The Pauli exclusion principle: never put two electrons in the identical state. Writing configurations this way explains the periodic table's 'blocks' — the s-block, p-block, the d-block (the transition metals), and the f-block — each block being the orbital type being filled there.
depths.deep: Orbital energies aren't ordered strictly by the number n. The 4s orbital fills before 3d because of 'penetration' (4s dips closer to the nucleus) and 'shielding' (inner electrons partly block the nuclear pull). Once 3d is occupied it often sinks below 4s in energy, which is why transition-metal ions lose their 4s electrons first when they form ions. A few elements (chromium, copper) break the simple pattern because a half-filled or completely filled subshell gains extra stability from a quantum effect called exchange energy.

atoms.title: The periodic table as organizing law
atoms.summary: Arranging elements by atomic number makes chemical properties recur periodically, because outer-shell structure repeats.

depths.eli5: There are about 118 known elements (the pure substances everything is made of). If you line them up in order of how many protons they have, something magical happens: their behavior starts to repeat in a regular pattern. Every so often you reach an element that acts a lot like an earlier one — a chemical 'cousin'. The periodic table is just that line-up, folded into rows so the cousins stack into columns.
depths.core: The periodic table arranges all the elements so that chemical behavior recurs in a regular ('periodic') way. The 19th-century chemist Dmitri Mendeleev first ordered elements so that families with similar reactivity fell in the same column, even leaving gaps for elements not yet discovered. The modern table orders strictly by atomic number Z (proton count). A column is called a group; a row is called a period. The repeating behavior is a direct shadow of electron configuration: elements in the same group have the same arrangement of outer electrons (their 'valence' electrons), and since outer electrons control bonding, same-group elements react alike.
depths.deep: The table is essentially a map of the solutions to the Schrödinger equation. The length of each period (2, 8, 8, 18, 18, 32) exactly equals the number of electrons the subshells being filled there can hold. The block structure (s, p, d, f) corresponds to which orbital-shape (the ℓ value) the most recently added electron occupies. In other words, the periodic law is quantum mechanics made visible on a wall chart.

quiz.prompt: What property are modern periodic tables ordered by?
quiz.answer: Atomic number (the number of protons, Z).

atoms.title: Periodic trends
atoms.summary: Atomic radius, ionization energy, electron affinity, and electronegativity vary smoothly across periods and down groups.

depths.eli5: Because the periodic table is so orderly, an element's properties change smoothly as you move across it. As you go left-to-right across a row, atoms get a little smaller and hold onto their electrons more tightly. As you go down a column, atoms get bigger and hold their outer electrons more loosely. Knowing these two simple directions lets you guess how an element behaves without memorizing each one.
depths.core: Periodic trends are the smooth changes in atomic properties across the table. The key ones: atomic radius (how big the atom is), ionization energy (how hard it is to pull an electron off), electron affinity (how much energy is released when the atom grabs an extra electron), and electronegativity (how strongly an atom pulls on shared electrons in a bond). Across a period, the nuclear charge (proton count) grows but the electrons are being added to the same outer shell, so the nucleus pulls everything in tighter: atoms shrink and ionization energy and electronegativity rise. Down a group, each step adds a whole new shell of electrons farther out, so the outermost electrons are easier to remove. These trends predict which atoms tend to give electrons away and which tend to take them — the heart of how bonds form.
depths.deep: The single quantity behind all these trends is the effective nuclear charge, Z_eff = Z − S: the net pull an outer electron actually feels once inner electrons (the 'shielding' S) partly cancel the nuclear charge Z. The trends have telling exceptions where subshell stability matters — for example the small dips in ionization energy at boron (after the 2s subshell just filled) and oxygen (after the 2p subshell became half-filled) directly reveal the underlying electron-pairing and exchange energetics.

quiz.prompt: How does atomic radius change going left-to-right across a period, and why?
quiz.answer: It decreases — increasing nuclear charge with constant shielding pulls the same shell inward.

quiz.prompt: Which has the higher first ionization energy, sodium or chlorine?
quiz.answer: Chlorine — it is farther right in the same period with higher Z_eff, so it holds electrons more tightly.

atoms.title: Effective nuclear charge
atoms.summary: An outer electron feels not the full nuclear charge but a reduced charge, screened by inner electrons.

depths.eli5: The nucleus tugs on every electron, but the outer electrons don't feel the full tug. The electrons packed in close to the nucleus form a crowd that partly blocks the pull — like people standing in front of you at a concert blocking your view of the stage. So an outer electron feels a watered-down version of the nucleus's pull. The equation Z_eff = Z − S just says: real felt pull = full charge minus the blocking.
depths.core: An atom's nucleus has a charge Z (equal to its number of protons), but an outer electron doesn't experience all of it. The inner-shell electrons repel the outer electron and partly cancel the nuclear pull — an effect called shielding, written S. The leftover pull the outer electron actually feels is the effective nuclear charge: Z_eff = Z − S. This one quantity explains a lot at once: how big atoms are, how much energy it takes to remove an electron (ionization energy), and why, moving across a period, the outer electrons get harder and harder to pull off (Z rises faster than S).
depths.deep: Shielding is imperfect and depends on orbital shape: s electrons 'penetrate' closer to the nucleus and shield well, p electrons less, d and f electrons poorly. Slater's rules are a simple recipe for estimating S by hand. The penetration ordering s > p > d > f is exactly why subshells within the same shell end up at slightly different energies, which in turn drives the order in which orbitals fill.

quiz.prompt: What is shielding?
quiz.answer: The partial cancellation of nuclear charge experienced by an outer electron due to repulsion from inner electrons.

quiz.answer: Added electrons go into the same valence shell and shield each other poorly, while Z rises by one each step, so S grows slower than Z and Z_eff = Z − S increases.

atoms.title: Ionic bonding
atoms.summary: A metal donates electrons to a nonmetal, and the resulting oppositely charged ions are held in a lattice by electrostatics.

depths.eli5: Atoms can hold together in different ways; this is one of them. One atom simply hands its spare outer electrons to a neighbor. Now the giver is short of electrons (positively charged) and the taker has extra (negatively charged). Opposite charges attract, so the two stick together hard. Table salt is held together exactly this way.
depths.core: A bond is the force that holds atoms together in a substance. In ionic bonding, electrons are transferred completely from one atom to another. This happens when an atom that gives up electrons easily (low ionization energy — typically a metal) meets one that grabs electrons readily (high electron affinity — typically a nonmetal). An atom that has lost electrons becomes a positively charged ion called a cation; one that has gained electrons becomes a negatively charged anion. Vast numbers of these ions stack into a regular, repeating 3-D pattern called a crystal lattice, with positives and negatives alternating. The total energy released by assembling that lattice is the lattice energy — the glue's strength. Ionic compounds are hard, brittle, and melt only at high temperatures; they conduct electricity only when melted or dissolved (when the ions are free to move).
depths.deep: Lattice energy scales roughly as q₁q₂/r — the product of the ion charges divided by their separation (Coulomb's law, made precise by the Born–Landé equation). So charge magnitude dominates: magnesium oxide (with 2+ and 2− ions) melts far higher than sodium chloride (1+ and 1−) even though the ions are similar in size. 'Purely ionic' is an idealization; real bonds always have some shared-electron (covalent) character, which grows when a small, highly charged cation distorts a large anion's electron cloud (summarized by Fajans' rules).

quiz.prompt: What holds an ionic crystal together?
quiz.answer: Electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions, quantified as the lattice energy.

quiz.prompt: Why does MgO have a much higher melting point than NaCl?
quiz.answer: Lattice energy scales with the product of ion charges; MgO's 2+/2− ions attract far more strongly than NaCl's 1+/1−.

atoms.title: Covalent bonding
atoms.summary: Two atoms share electron pairs, lowering energy by letting electrons feel both nuclei at once.

depths.eli5: Here's the other main way atoms stick together. Instead of one atom handing electrons over, two atoms hold a pair of electrons in the gap between them — like two kids holding the same rope. That shared pair tugs on both atoms at once and pulls them together. Most of the molecules in living things (water, sugar, DNA) are built from bonds like this.
depths.core: In a covalent bond, two atoms share one or more pairs of electrons rather than transferring them. This happens when neither atom can easily lose or gain electrons outright — typically between two nonmetals. A shared electron pair sitting between the two nuclei is attracted to both positive nuclei at once, which lowers the total energy and locks the atoms together (lower energy = more stable). Atoms tend to keep sharing until each reaches a stable, full count of outer electrons — usually eight, the 'octet rule'. Sharing one pair gives a single bond, two pairs a double bond, three pairs a triple bond. More shared pairs make a shorter, stronger bond.
depths.deep: The energy drop is genuinely quantum-mechanical: the electron 'waves' of the two atoms add together (constructive interference) and pile up electron density between the nuclei. The dominant reason energy falls is that the shared electron spreads out (delocalizes) over both atoms, which lowers its kinetic energy. The number of shared pairs is the bond order (1, 2, or 3), and higher bond order tracks with shorter, stronger bonds.

quiz.prompt: What is shared in a covalent bond?
quiz.answer: One or more pairs of electrons, occupying the region between the two bonded nuclei.

quiz.prompt: Explain why a shared electron pair lowers the energy of two atoms.
quiz.answer: The shared electrons feel the attraction of both nuclei and delocalize over both atoms, which lowers their energy below that of the separated atoms.

atoms.title: Electronegativity and bond polarity
atoms.summary: Unequal electron-attracting power between bonded atoms creates partial charges and a continuum from covalent to ionic.

depths.eli5: When two atoms share electrons in a bond, they rarely share fairly. One atom usually pulls the shared electrons closer to itself. The stronger puller ends up a little bit negative (it has the electrons more), and the weaker one ends up a little bit positive. So even a shared bond can have a 'plus end' and a 'minus end' — like a tiny magnet.
depths.core: Electronegativity is a number that measures how strongly an atom pulls on the electrons in a bond. Compare the two atoms in a bond: if their electronegativities are nearly equal, they share evenly — a nonpolar covalent bond. If one pulls noticeably harder, the electrons sit closer to it, giving a polar bond with small partial charges, written δ− (slightly negative) on the stronger puller and δ+ (slightly positive) on the other. If the difference is huge, the pull becomes a complete grab — that's an ionic bond. So electronegativity difference is a sliding scale from nonpolar, to polar, to ionic. Bond polarity controls a molecule's solubility, the weak attractions between molecules, and where it tends to react.
depths.deep: Because the covalent-to-ionic change is a smooth continuum, not two separate categories, chemists use scales like Pauling's (derived from measured bond energies). Polarity at the whole-molecule level is captured by the dipole moment, μ = q·d (charge times separation), which depends on geometry. A molecule can have polar bonds yet be nonpolar overall if those bond dipoles point in opposite directions and cancel — carbon dioxide (CO₂) is the classic example because it is linear.

quiz.prompt: What does electronegativity measure?
quiz.answer: The tendency of an atom to attract the shared electrons in a chemical bond.

quiz.prompt: CO₂ has two polar C=O bonds but no net dipole. Why?
quiz.answer: It is linear, so the two bond dipoles point in opposite directions and cancel.

atoms.title: Lewis structures and the octet rule
atoms.summary: Dot-and-line diagrams track valence electrons as bonds and lone pairs, with most main-group atoms seeking eight.

depths.eli5: Chemists use a simple drawing to picture a molecule. You draw each atom's outer electrons as dots, then pair the dots up — a shared pair becomes a line (a bond). The goal is to arrange things so every atom is surrounded by a full set of eight outer electrons (hydrogen is happy with two). This sketch is called a Lewis structure, and it tells you how the atoms are connected.
depths.core: A Lewis structure is a bookkeeping diagram of a molecule's outer (valence) electrons. You count all the valence electrons available, then place them either as bonding pairs (shared between two atoms, drawn as lines) or lone pairs (sitting on a single atom, drawn as dots). You check that each main-group atom has eight outer electrons — the octet rule — except hydrogen, which only needs two. When more than one valid drawing is possible, formal charge (a simple count comparing an atom's electrons in the structure to its normal count) tells you which is best. Resonance is used when the electrons are actually spread (delocalized) over several equivalent arrangements; you draw each and understand the real molecule as a blend.
depths.deep: The octet rule is a useful rule of thumb, not an unbreakable law. It works because an atom's outer s and p orbitals together hold eight electrons. Genuine exceptions exist: electron-deficient molecules like boron trifluoride (BF₃, only six around boron), odd-electron radicals like nitric oxide (NO), and 'expanded octets' like sulfur hexafluoride (SF₆, twelve around sulfur). The expanded cases — called hypervalency — are now explained by very polar bonding rather than the older idea of filling d orbitals.

quiz.prompt: What is the octet rule?
quiz.answer: Main-group atoms tend to gain, lose, or share electrons to achieve eight valence electrons (a noble-gas configuration).

quiz.prompt: Name one molecule that violates the octet rule and how.
quiz.answer: SF₆ has an expanded octet (12 electrons around sulfur); BF₃ is electron-deficient (only 6 around boron); NO is an odd-electron radical.

atoms.title: VSEPR and molecular geometry
atoms.summary: Electron-pair domains around a central atom repel and spread out, fixing molecular shape.

depths.eli5: Molecules aren't flat blobs — they have definite 3-D shapes, and shape decides how a molecule behaves. Here's the trick to predicting it: around the central atom, each clump of electrons repels every other clump and they spread out as far from each other as they can, exactly like balloons tied together at one knot push apart. Wherever the clumps end up pointing is the molecule's shape.
depths.core: VSEPR stands for Valence-Shell Electron-Pair Repulsion. The idea: around a central atom, count the 'domains' of electrons — each bonded group counts as one domain, and each lone pair (an unshared pair sitting on the atom) counts as one too. These domains push apart to get as far from each other as possible, which fixes the geometry: 2 domains give a straight line (linear), 3 give a flat triangle (trigonal planar), 4 give a tetrahedron (tetrahedral, 109.5° angles), 5 give a trigonal bipyramid, 6 give an octahedron. Lone pairs take up a bit more room than bonds, so they squeeze the bond angles slightly — which is why water is bent at 104.5° instead of the ideal 109.5°.
depths.deep: VSEPR predicts shapes remarkably well using nothing but an electron count, but it is a model, not the true cause. The deeper reason electron pairs avoid each other is the Pauli principle (same-spin electrons cannot occupy the same state) combined with plain electrostatic repulsion. VSEPR pairs naturally with the idea of hybridization, which describes which orbitals the atom uses to point its bonds in those directions.

quiz.answer: Tetrahedral, with ideal angles of 109.5°.

atoms.title: Orbital hybridization
atoms.summary: Atomic orbitals mix into equivalent hybrid orbitals that point toward bonding partners, matching observed geometry.

depths.eli5: An atom's basic electron 'rooms' (orbitals) come in different shapes and don't all point the right way for bonding. So the atom blends them into a fresh set of identical, evenly-spaced rooms that aim straight at its neighbors. With matching rooms pointing the right directions, the bonds all come out the same and the molecule gets a clean symmetric shape.
depths.core: Hybridization describes how an atom mixes its basic atomic orbitals into a new set of equivalent 'hybrid' orbitals aimed at its bonding partners. Example: in methane (CH₄), carbon mixes its one 2s orbital and three 2p orbitals into four identical sp³ hybrids that point to the corners of a tetrahedron, giving four equal C–H bonds. Mixing the s with only two p orbitals gives three sp² hybrids in a flat triangle (trigonal planar), leaving one unmixed p orbital available to form a second, side-by-side bond called a π bond. Mixing s with one p gives two sp hybrids in a straight line, leaving two unmixed p orbitals. So hybridization is the orbital-level partner of VSEPR: VSEPR predicts the shape, hybridization names the orbitals that produce it. (A normal end-to-end single bond is called a σ bond.)
depths.deep: Hybridization is a mathematical change of description, not a physical event the atom 'does' — it is the combination of atomic orbitals that best matches the molecule's symmetry, and it conveniently splits the bonding into a σ framework (from the hybrids) and a π system (from leftover unmixed p orbitals). It is descriptive rather than predictive: experiments like photoelectron spectroscopy show the underlying orbitals are not literally all identical, so hybridization is best treated as a useful model.

quiz.answer: sp (two hybrid orbitals 180° apart).

atoms.title: Molecular orbital theory
atoms.summary: Atomic orbitals combine into delocalized bonding and antibonding molecular orbitals filled by all the molecule's electrons.

depths.eli5: Here's a more powerful way to picture bonding. When atoms join, their separate electron 'rooms' (orbitals) merge into new rooms that belong to the whole molecule. Some of these new rooms hold electrons in the gap between atoms and act like glue (bonding); others put electrons where they actually push the atoms apart (antibonding). Whether a molecule holds together depends on which kind the electrons fill.
depths.core: Molecular orbital (MO) theory treats a molecule's electrons as belonging to the whole molecule, not to individual atoms. When you combine N atomic orbitals you get N molecular orbitals. The 'in-phase' combinations are bonding orbitals — lower energy, with electron density piled between the nuclei (stabilizing). The 'out-of-phase' combinations are antibonding orbitals — higher energy, with a node (a gap of zero electron density) between the nuclei (destabilizing). The net bonding is captured by the bond order = ½ (bonding electrons − antibonding electrons). MO theory explains things the simpler Lewis-dot picture cannot: why oxygen (O₂) is paramagnetic (weakly attracted to a magnet because it has unpaired electrons), why some molecules have fractional bond orders, and why a helium molecule (He₂) never forms.
depths.deep: MO theory is the 'linear combination of atomic orbitals' (LCAO) approximation to the molecular Schrödinger equation. You fill the molecular orbitals from lowest energy up — Aufbau again — which directly predicts spectra and magnetism. For O₂, the two highest electrons land in a pair of equal-energy antibonding (π*) orbitals with parallel spins (Hund's rule), giving two unpaired electrons and hence its magnetic behavior, a result Lewis structures get wrong.

quiz.prompt: How is bond order defined in MO theory?
quiz.answer: Bond order = ½ (number of bonding electrons − number of antibonding electrons).

quiz.prompt: Why does He₂ not form a stable bond?
quiz.answer: Its four electrons fill both the bonding and antibonding σ orbitals, giving bond order ½(2−2)=0, so there is no net bonding.

atoms.title: Metallic bonding
atoms.summary: Metal atoms pool their valence electrons into a delocalized sea (or bands) shared across the whole lattice.

depths.eli5: Metals like copper and iron hold together a third way. The outer electrons don't belong to any single atom — they all let go and roam freely through the whole chunk of metal, like a shared swimming pool of electrons sloshing around fixed positive cores. Because the electrons can move anywhere, metals carry electricity, and because nothing locks the cores into rigid positions, you can bend and hammer metal without it shattering.
depths.core: In metallic bonding, every metal atom releases its outer (valence) electrons into a shared, collective pool — often called the 'electron sea' — that flows freely around a fixed lattice of positive cores (cations). Because the electrons are delocalized (not tied to one atom), this picture explains the signature properties of metals: they conduct electricity and heat well (the free electrons carry charge and energy), they are malleable and ductile (you can bend or stretch them because the cores slide past each other without snapping any directional bond), and they have a shiny metallic luster (the free electrons reflect light).
depths.deep: The electron-sea idea is the simple limit of a deeper picture called band theory: when many atomic orbitals overlap across a huge number of atoms, their energy levels merge into continuous 'bands'. Electrical conduction happens when a band is only partly filled, so electrons have nearby empty states to move into. The size of the gap (if any) between the filled valence band and the empty conduction band is exactly what separates metals (no gap), semiconductors (small gap), and insulators (large gap).

quiz.prompt: What is the 'electron sea' in a metal?
quiz.answer: The delocalized valence electrons shared collectively among all the metal cations in the lattice.

quiz.prompt: Explain why metals conduct electricity and are malleable.
quiz.answer: Delocalized electrons move freely to carry current; because bonding is nondirectional, cores can slide past one another under stress without snapping bonds.

atoms.title: The mole and Avogadro's number
atoms.summary: A mole is a fixed count of particles that links the atomic scale to gram-scale laboratory amounts.

depths.eli5: Atoms are so tiny that there are mind-bending numbers of them in even a pinch of stuff — far too many to count one by one. So chemists invented a counting word for a fixed, huge batch of them: the mole. Just like 'a dozen' always means 12, 'a mole' always means 6.022×10²³ (that's 602 followed by 21 zeros). With a counting word this size, you can weigh out a known number of atoms on a scale.
depths.core: A mole is a fixed count of particles: 6.022×10²³ of them, a value called Avogadro's number (N_A). It bridges the invisible world of atoms and the everyday world of grams. The trick is molar mass: the mass in grams of one mole of a substance is numerically equal to its average atomic or molecular mass (the number you read off the periodic table). So one mole of carbon weighs about 12 grams; one mole of water weighs about 18 grams. This lets a chemist weigh a sample and immediately know how many particles it holds — the foundation of doing chemistry by the numbers.
depths.deep: Since the 2019 redefinition of the international system of units (SI), Avogadro's number is a defined exact constant (6.02214076×10²³ per mole) rather than something measured experimentally, so the mole is now defined purely as that fixed particle count. Molar mass is still tied to atomic masses, which are themselves weighted averages over an element's naturally occurring isotopes (atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons).

quiz.answer: 6.022×10²³, the number of particles in one mole.

atoms.title: Stoichiometry and balanced equations
atoms.summary: Balanced chemical equations fix the mole ratios that convert amounts of reactants into amounts of products.

depths.eli5: A chemical reaction is like a cooking recipe written with symbols. A 'balanced equation' is a recipe where the ingredients (reactants) on the left turn into results (products) on the right, with the numbers worked out so that every atom is accounted for — nothing is created or destroyed, atoms just get rearranged. The numbers in front tell you exactly how many of each ingredient you need.
depths.core: Stoichiometry is the math of how much reacts with how much. A chemical equation shows reactants turning into products, e.g. 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O. Balancing it means choosing the numbers in front (the coefficients) so the same count of each kind of atom appears on both sides — this enforces conservation of mass (matter is neither created nor destroyed). Those coefficients are mole ratios: they tell you the proportions in which substances combine, and act as conversion factors between any two substances in the reaction. With them you can predict how much product forms, find the limiting reagent (the ingredient that runs out first and caps the amount of product), and compute the percent yield (how much you actually got versus the theoretical maximum).
depths.deep: Stoichiometry is bookkeeping forced by the conservation of atoms (and, for charged species, charge). For redox reactions — where electrons move — you must also balance the electrons transferred. The limiting reagent is whichever runs out first relative to its coefficient; it alone sets the theoretical yield, and whatever is left over is the 'excess' reagent.

quiz.answer: The mole ratios in which reactants combine and products form.

quiz.answer: H₂ — it needs O₂ in a 2:1 ratio, so 3 mol H₂ requires only 1.5 mol O₂; H₂ runs out first.

atoms.title: The ideal gas law
atoms.summary: Pressure, volume, amount, and temperature of a dilute gas obey one combined relation.

depths.eli5: Gases respond to squeezing and heating in simple ways: squeeze a gas into a smaller space and its pressure (the push on the container walls) goes up; warm it and it either pushes harder or expands. One neat formula, PV = nRT, ties together pressure (P), volume (V), the amount of gas (n), and temperature (T) all at once.
depths.core: The ideal gas law, PV = nRT, relates the four things that describe a gas: pressure P, volume V, amount n (in moles), and absolute temperature T (measured from absolute zero, in kelvin). R is a fixed number called the gas constant. The law bundles three older observations: at fixed amount, pressure and volume are inversely related (Boyle's law — squeeze to half the volume, double the pressure); volume grows with temperature (Charles's law); and equal volumes of gas hold equal numbers of molecules at the same P and T (Avogadro's law). It pictures gas molecules as tiny points that don't attract each other — a very good approximation when the gas is dilute (low pressure, high temperature).
depths.deep: PV = nRT can be derived from the kinetic theory of gases: pressure is the cumulative push from molecules colliding with the walls, and absolute temperature is a measure of their average kinetic energy. Real gases deviate from the ideal law when molecules are crowded enough that their own size and their mutual attractions matter; the van der Waals equation, (P + a n²/V²)(V − nb) = nRT, patches in corrections for both effects.

atoms.title: Kinetic-molecular theory
atoms.summary: Gas behavior follows from many tiny particles in constant random motion whose average kinetic energy is set by temperature.

depths.eli5: Zoom in on a gas and it's a huge swarm of tiny balls (the molecules) zooming around in all directions and bouncing off the walls of their container. The constant drumming of these bounces is what we feel as pressure, and how fast the balls zoom on average is what we measure as temperature. Hotter = faster.
depths.core: Kinetic-molecular theory explains where the gas laws come from by modeling a gas as countless tiny molecules in constant, random motion. The assumptions: the molecules are very small compared to the space between them, they don't attract each other, and their collisions are 'elastic' (no energy lost). From these, two key ideas follow: pressure is the combined force of molecules hammering the container walls, and absolute temperature is directly proportional to the molecules' average kinetic energy of motion. The molecules don't all move at one speed — their speeds are spread out in a predictable pattern called the Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution.
depths.deep: The central result is ½m⟨v²⟩ = (3/2)k_BT (average kinetic energy is set by temperature, where k_B is the Boltzmann constant). This means average speed scales as the square root of T/M, so lighter molecules move faster at the same temperature. That explains effusion rates (how fast a gas leaks through a tiny hole — Graham's law) and why light hydrogen escapes a planet's gravity while heavier CO₂ stays. The high-speed 'tail' of the distribution — the small fraction of unusually fast, energetic molecules — is exactly what drives the rates of chemical reactions.

quiz.prompt: What does absolute temperature correspond to in kinetic-molecular theory?
quiz.answer: The average translational kinetic energy of the molecules.

quiz.answer: Helium — lighter molecules have higher average speed since ½m⟨v²⟩ is the same, so ⟨v²⟩ ∝ 1/m.

atoms.title: Intermolecular forces
atoms.summary: Attractions between whole molecules — dispersion, dipole-dipole, and hydrogen bonding — set boiling points and phase behavior.

depths.eli5: There are strong forces holding the atoms inside a molecule together — but there are also much weaker forces of attraction between whole, separate molecules. Even molecules with no overall charge feel a faint stickiness toward their neighbors. The stickier the molecules, the more energy it takes to pull them apart, so the higher the boiling point.
depths.core: Intermolecular forces are the attractions between separate molecules (as opposed to the bonds inside a molecule). There are three main kinds, from weakest to strongest. London dispersion forces exist between all molecules: at any instant an electron cloud can be lopsided, creating a fleeting tiny dipole (a plus end and a minus end) that pulls on a neighbor; these grow stronger as molecules get bigger. Dipole-dipole forces act between permanently polar molecules (ones with a fixed plus and minus end), which line up plus-to-minus. Hydrogen bonding is the strongest: it occurs when a hydrogen atom bonded to nitrogen, oxygen, or fluorine is attracted to a lone pair on a nearby N, O, or F. Together these forces set boiling points, viscosity (thickness), and surface tension.
depths.deep: All three are ultimately electrostatic, but differ in range and strength; dispersion comes from correlated quantum fluctuations of electron clouds and falls off as r⁻⁶ (very fast with distance). Hydrogen bonding is why water boils about 160 °C higher than its small mass would predict, and it is the organizing force behind liquid water's structure, how proteins fold into shape, and how the two strands of DNA pair up.

quiz.prompt: Which intermolecular force is present in all substances?
quiz.answer: London dispersion forces (induced-dipole / induced-dipole).

quiz.prompt: Why does water have an unusually high boiling point for its molecular mass?
quiz.answer: Extensive hydrogen bonding between water molecules requires extra energy to overcome before boiling.

atoms.title: States of matter and phase transitions
atoms.summary: Solid, liquid, and gas reflect the contest between intermolecular attraction and thermal motion, mapped by a phase diagram.

depths.eli5: Water can be ice, liquid, or steam — same molecules, just different amounts of energy. When molecules are cold they barely move and lock into a rigid solid; warm them and they loosen into a flowing liquid; heat them more and they break free entirely as a gas. It's a tug-of-war between the molecules' stickiness (which wants to hold them together) and their heat energy (which wants to fling them apart).
depths.core: The three common states of matter — solid, liquid, and gas — reflect a contest between intermolecular attraction (the stickiness holding molecules together) and thermal energy (random motion, which increases with temperature T). When stickiness wins you get a solid; as heat wins out you progress to liquid then gas. A phase diagram is a map that shows which state is stable at any given pressure and temperature, with lines marking where transitions happen. Two special spots appear on it: the triple point, the unique pressure and temperature where solid, liquid, and gas all coexist; and the critical point, beyond which the liquid and gas blur into one and can no longer be told apart.
depths.deep: A phase transition occurs where the 'free energy' (a stability measure) of two phases becomes equal; at that boundary the molar Gibbs energies of the two phases match. The Clausius–Clapeyron relation gives the slope of the liquid–gas (vapor-pressure) line on the diagram. Past the critical point the liquid/gas distinction vanishes into a supercritical fluid — a state with in-between properties that's used as an environmentally friendly 'green' solvent, for example to decaffeinate coffee with supercritical CO₂.

quiz.prompt: What is the triple point on a phase diagram?
quiz.answer: The unique pressure and temperature where solid, liquid, and gas phases all coexist in equilibrium.

quiz.prompt: Explain in energy terms why heating a solid eventually makes it a gas.
quiz.answer: Adding thermal energy increases molecular motion until it overcomes the intermolecular attractions holding molecules in fixed (solid) then close (liquid) arrangements, finally freeing them as a gas.

atoms.title: Solutions and concentration
atoms.summary: A solute dissolves in a solvent when their intermolecular interactions are compatible, with concentration measured in molarity.

depths.eli5: When you stir sugar into water and it disappears, that's dissolving — a solution. The thing that dissolves (sugar) is the solute; the liquid it dissolves into (water) is the solvent. Things dissolve when they 'get along' with the liquid: salt and sugar love water, but oil refuses to mix with it. 'Concentration' is just a way of saying how crowded the dissolved stuff is.
depths.core: A solution is a uniform mixture of a solute (the dissolved substance) in a solvent (the dissolving liquid). Whether something dissolves follows the rule 'like dissolves like': polar and ionic solutes (with charged or lopsided molecules) dissolve in polar solvents like water, while nonpolar solutes dissolve in nonpolar solvents like oil. Dissolving means trading the attractions among solute particles and among solvent particles for new attractions between solute and solvent. Concentration is most often given as molarity — moles of solute per liter of solution (mol/L) — a number that plugs directly into stoichiometry and equilibrium calculations.
depths.deep: Whether a substance dissolves depends on the Gibbs free energy of mixing, which usually has a large favorable entropy (disorder) term pushing things to mix. For an ionic solid, dissolving is a close contest between the lattice energy holding the crystal together (a cost) and the hydration energy released when water surrounds the freed ions (a payoff). Once dissolved, the solute produces colligative properties — boiling-point elevation, freezing-point depression, and osmotic pressure — that depend only on how many dissolved particles there are, not what they are.

quiz.answer: Solutes dissolve best in solvents with similar polarity — polar/ionic in polar solvents, nonpolar in nonpolar.

atoms.title: Enthalpy and heats of reaction
atoms.summary: Enthalpy change is the heat exchanged at constant pressure, negative for exothermic and positive for endothermic reactions.

depths.eli5: Reactions move heat around. Some give off heat — you feel the beaker get warm, like a hand-warmer. Others soak heat up and go cold, like an instant cold-pack. 'Enthalpy' is just the accounting word for tracking that heat. A reaction's enthalpy change tells you how much heat it released or absorbed.
depths.core: Enthalpy (symbol H) is a measure of a substance's heat content. What chemists usually care about is the enthalpy change of a reaction, written ΔH (the Greek delta means 'change in'). At constant pressure — the normal condition in an open lab — ΔH equals the heat the reaction exchanges with its surroundings. A reaction that releases heat is exothermic, and it has ΔH < 0 (negative), which happens because the new bonds in the products are more stable (lower energy) than the bonds in the reactants. A reaction that absorbs heat is endothermic, with ΔH > 0 (positive). Because enthalpy is a state function (it depends only on the start and end, not the route taken), Hess's law lets you add up the enthalpy changes of separate steps to get the overall ΔH.
depths.deep: Formally H = U + PV, where U is internal energy; the PV term is why heat measured at constant pressure (ΔH) differs from heat at constant volume (ΔU) by the work done pushing back the surroundings as the system expands. Chemists tabulate standard enthalpies of formation — the ΔH to make one mole of a compound from its pure elements — and then compute any reaction's enthalpy as ΔH°_rxn = Σ ΔH°_f(products) − Σ ΔH°_f(reactants).

quiz.prompt: What is the sign of ΔH for an exothermic reaction?
quiz.answer: Negative (ΔH < 0) — heat is released to the surroundings.

quiz.prompt: Using Hess's law, why can you add the enthalpies of two steps to get the enthalpy of an overall reaction?
quiz.answer: Enthalpy is a state function, so ΔH depends only on initial and final states, not the path — step enthalpies add to the overall value.

atoms.title: Entropy and the second law
atoms.summary: Entropy measures the number of microscopic arrangements, and isolated systems evolve toward higher total entropy.

depths.eli5: Entropy is a measure of how many different ways the bits of something can be arranged while still looking the same overall. There are far more messy, spread-out arrangements than tidy ones, so things naturally drift toward being spread out — that's why a drop of dye disperses through water and never gathers back into a drop on its own. Nature tends toward the arrangement that can happen the most ways.
depths.core: Entropy (symbol S) counts how many microscopic arrangements ('microstates', W) are consistent with what you actually observe. Boltzmann's equation S = k ln W (k is the Boltzmann constant) makes this precise: more possible arrangements means higher entropy. The second law of thermodynamics says that in any spontaneous (self-occurring) process, the total entropy of the universe — the system plus its surroundings — increases. This is why gases expand to fill a room, heat flows from hot to cold, and dissolved substances spread out evenly: each of these moves toward the state that can be realized in vastly more ways.
depths.deep: Entropy is not vaguely 'messiness' — it is a precise count of accessible microstates. A reaction can lower the system's own entropy and still be spontaneous if it releases enough heat to raise the surroundings' entropy by more (ΔS_surr = −ΔH/T, where heat dumped at lower temperature raises entropy most). That trade-off between system and surroundings is exactly what the Gibbs free energy criterion repackages into a convenient system-only test.

quiz.answer: The number of microstates (microscopic arrangements) consistent with the system's macrostate.

quiz.prompt: How can a reaction that lowers the system's entropy still be spontaneous?
quiz.answer: If it releases heat, it raises the surroundings' entropy (ΔS_surr = −ΔH/T); spontaneity requires the total entropy of system plus surroundings to increase.

atoms.title: Gibbs free energy
atoms.summary: At constant temperature and pressure, a process is spontaneous when its Gibbs free energy change is negative.

depths.eli5: Wouldn't it be handy to have one number that tells you whether a reaction will happen by itself? Gibbs free energy is that number. If a reaction's Gibbs free energy goes down (the change is negative), the reaction is 'downhill' and will proceed on its own. If it would go up, the reaction won't happen unless you push it.
depths.core: Gibbs free energy (symbol G) bundles two competing tendencies — releasing heat (enthalpy) and increasing disorder (entropy) — into a single spontaneity test that works at constant temperature and pressure: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS. Here ΔH is the enthalpy change, ΔS the entropy change, and T the absolute temperature. The rule: ΔG < 0 means the process is spontaneous (it can happen on its own); ΔG > 0 means it is nonspontaneous (the reverse is favored); ΔG = 0 means the system is at equilibrium (balanced). Temperature T is the dial that decides whether the entropy term (TΔS) can outweigh the enthalpy term, which is why some reactions only 'go' when heated.
depths.deep: ΔG also equals the maximum useful (non-expansion) work a process can deliver, and it is just the second law restated in a system-only form (ΔG = −T·ΔS_universe at constant T and P). It is the central hinge of chemical thermodynamics because it connects to equilibrium through ΔG° = −RT ln K and to electrochemistry (batteries) through ΔG° = −nFE°.

quiz.prompt: What sign of ΔG indicates a spontaneous process?
quiz.answer: Negative (ΔG < 0).

quiz.prompt: A reaction has ΔH > 0 and ΔS > 0. Under what condition is it spontaneous?
quiz.answer: When TΔS exceeds ΔH, i.e., at high enough temperature, so ΔG = ΔH − TΔS becomes negative.

atoms.title: Chemical equilibrium and K
atoms.summary: A reversible reaction settles at a ratio of products to reactants fixed by the equilibrium constant K.

depths.eli5: Many reactions never fully finish. Instead they reach a steady mixture of leftover reactants and freshly made products and then just sit there, seemingly unchanged. This balance point is called equilibrium, and K is a single number that tells you where the balance lands — mostly products, mostly reactants, or somewhere in between.
depths.core: A reversible reaction can run forward (reactants → products) and backward (products → reactants) at the same time. At equilibrium the forward and reverse rates become equal, so the amounts of everything stop changing (even though molecules keep reacting both ways). The equilibrium constant K captures the balance: it is the ratio of product 'activities' to reactant 'activities' (activity = effective concentration), each raised to the power of its coefficient in the balanced equation. A large K means equilibrium favors products; a small K means it favors reactants. To predict which way a mixture that's not yet at equilibrium will move, you compute the reaction quotient Q (the same ratio using the current amounts) and compare it to K: the reaction shifts in whichever direction brings Q toward K.
depths.deep: K is fixed by thermodynamics through ΔG° = −RT ln K, so it depends only on temperature — not on how much you start with and not on whether a catalyst is present. Equilibrium is dynamic, not frozen: molecules keep converting in both directions at matched rates. In nonideal (crowded) systems, 'activities' replace plain concentrations to make K rigorous.

quiz.prompt: What does a large value of K tell you about a reaction at equilibrium?
quiz.answer: Equilibrium strongly favors products (high product concentration relative to reactants).

quiz.prompt: If the reaction quotient Q is greater than K, which direction does the reaction proceed?
quiz.answer: In reverse, toward reactants, until Q falls to K.

atoms.title: Le Chatelier's principle
atoms.summary: A system at equilibrium responds to a disturbance by shifting in the direction that partially offsets the change.

depths.eli5: A reaction sitting at its balance point (equilibrium) acts a bit like a stubborn seesaw: push on it and it pushes back. If you dump in more of one ingredient, the reaction responds by using some of it up; if you take something away, it makes more. It always shifts in the direction that partly undoes whatever you did.
depths.core: Le Chatelier's principle predicts how a reaction at equilibrium responds to a disturbance: it shifts in the direction that partially offsets the change. Three common disturbances: (1) Concentration — add more reactant and equilibrium shifts toward products to consume it (remove a product and it shifts the same way). (2) Pressure — compress a gas mixture and equilibrium shifts toward the side with fewer gas molecules, easing the squeeze. (3) Temperature — treat heat as a reactant for an endothermic reaction or a product for an exothermic one; adding heat shifts away from it. Importantly, the system settles into a new equilibrium, not the original one.
depths.deep: The principle is qualitative shorthand for how the reaction quotient Q gets nudged relative to the equilibrium constant K. Changing concentration or pressure moves Q while K stays fixed, so the reaction re-balances Q back to K. Only temperature actually changes K itself (through ΔG° = −RT ln K and the van't Hoff relation). A catalyst speeds the forward and reverse reactions equally, so it reaches equilibrium faster but never shifts where the equilibrium sits.

quiz.prompt: How does adding more reactant affect an equilibrium?
quiz.answer: It shifts the equilibrium toward products to consume the added reactant.

quiz.prompt: For an exothermic reaction, what happens to the position of equilibrium if you raise the temperature?
quiz.answer: It shifts toward reactants (and K decreases), since heat acts like a product and the system opposes the added heat.

atoms.title: Acids and bases
atoms.summary: Brønsted acids donate protons and bases accept them, reacting through conjugate acid-base pairs.

depths.eli5: Acids (like vinegar or lemon juice) and bases (like baking soda or soap) are opposites. The simplest way to tell them apart: an acid gives away hydrogen ions (a hydrogen atom stripped of its electron, written H⁺), and a base grabs them. They always come in matched pairs — a giver and a taker — and when they meet they neutralize each other.
depths.core: The most useful definition is the Brønsted–Lowry model: an acid is a proton donor (a proton here means H⁺, a hydrogen ion) and a base is a proton acceptor. When an acid gives up its proton, what's left is its conjugate base; when a base accepts one, it becomes its conjugate acid — so acids and bases always work in conjugate pairs. Strong acids hand off their protons completely in water; weak acids do so only partially, and how far is measured by the acid-dissociation constant K_a. A broader definition, the Lewis model, generalizes acids and bases to electron-pair acceptors and donors, covering reactions with no proton at all.
depths.deep: Acid strength is really the equilibrium position of proton transfer, captured by K_a (often reported as pK_a = −log K_a, where a lower pK_a means a stronger acid). A strong acid has a weak conjugate base and vice versa. For any conjugate pair, K_a·K_b = K_w, the water constant. Water itself is amphoteric — it can both donate and accept protons — which it does in a tiny amount even in pure water (autoionization).

quiz.prompt: Define a Brønsted–Lowry acid and base.
quiz.answer: An acid is a proton (H⁺) donor; a base is a proton acceptor.

quiz.prompt: What is the conjugate base of HCO₃⁻ when it acts as an acid?
quiz.answer: CO₃²⁻ (carbonate), formed when HCO₃⁻ donates a proton.

atoms.title: pH and the water equilibrium
atoms.summary: pH is a logarithmic measure of hydrogen-ion concentration, with the water autoionization product fixing the neutral point.

depths.eli5: pH is the familiar 0-to-14 ruler for how acidic or basic something is. Low numbers (like lemon juice at 2) are strong acids and taste sour; 7 in the middle is neutral, like pure water; high numbers (like bleach at 13) are strong bases and feel slippery. Each step on the ruler is a tenfold change — pH 3 is ten times more acidic than pH 4.
depths.core: Acidity is set by the concentration of hydrogen ions, written [H⁺], in a solution. That concentration can span an enormous range, so instead of huge or tiny numbers we use a compressed scale: pH = −log₁₀[H⁺] (the negative base-10 logarithm). Pure water slightly splits itself into H⁺ and OH⁻ ions (autoionization), and the product of their concentrations is fixed: K_w = [H⁺][OH⁻] = 1.0×10⁻¹⁴ at 25 °C. Taking logs gives pH + pOH = 14. So pH 7 is neutral, below 7 is acidic, above 7 is basic — and because it's a logarithm, each whole-number step is a tenfold change in [H⁺].
depths.deep: K_w depends on temperature, so 'neutral pH' is exactly 7 only at 25 °C; at other temperatures the neutral point shifts even though the water is still neutral (equal H⁺ and OH⁻). Strictly, pH is defined using hydrogen-ion activity (effective concentration) rather than raw concentration, which is why a measured pH in concentrated solutions can drift away from the simple −log[H⁺] value.

atoms.title: Buffers and the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation
atoms.summary: A weak acid and its conjugate base together resist pH change when small amounts of acid or base are added.

depths.eli5: A buffer is a chemical shock absorber for acidity. It keeps both an acid and its partner base on hand at the same time, so whatever you splash in — extra acid or extra base — gets soaked up and the pH (the acidity level) barely budges. Your blood is buffered this way, which is why its acidity stays remarkably steady.
depths.core: A buffer is a solution that resists changes in pH. It is made of a weak acid (call it HA) together with its conjugate base (A⁻) in comparable amounts. If you add acid, the A⁻ mops it up; if you add base, the HA neutralizes it — so the pH moves only a little. The Henderson–Hasselbalch equation, pH = pK_a + log([A⁻]/[HA]), gives the buffer's pH directly from the acid's pK_a (its strength) and the ratio of base to acid present. A buffer works best when that ratio is near 1, which happens when the pH is close to the pK_a.
depths.deep: A buffer's capacity — how much acid or base it can absorb before failing — is finite and peaks when pH = pK_a, staying effective within roughly ±1 pH unit of it. The Henderson–Hasselbalch equation is an approximation, valid when the buffer's concentrations are much larger than the amount of acid or base added. This chemistry is the operational backbone of blood pH control (the carbonic-acid/bicarbonate system) and of nearly every biochemistry experiment, where keeping pH constant is essential.

atoms.title: Reaction rate and rate laws
atoms.summary: The speed of a reaction depends on concentrations raised to experimentally determined orders.

depths.eli5: Some reactions are over in a flash, others crawl for years. How fast one runs usually depends on how crowded the reactants are. But you can't guess the exact relationship — doubling a reactant might double the speed, or quadruple it, or change nothing at all. You have to measure it in the lab.
depths.core: Reaction rate is how fast reactants turn into products. A rate law is the equation that links that speed to the concentrations of the reactants: rate = k[A]^m[B]^n. Here k is the rate constant (a number specific to the reaction and temperature), and the exponents m and n are the reaction orders — they say how sensitive the rate is to each reactant. Crucially, the orders are found by experiment, not read off the balanced equation's coefficients, because they reflect the actual step-by-step pathway (the mechanism). 'Integrated' rate laws then predict how concentration drops over time and give each reaction order a characteristic fingerprint, such as how its half-life behaves.
depths.deep: The rate law mirrors the slowest step in the mechanism — the rate-determining step — so the measured order encodes information about that step. A first-order reaction has a constant half-life (t½ = ln2/k) that doesn't depend on concentration — the very same mathematics as radioactive decay. A second-order reaction's half-life instead grows longer as the reaction proceeds and reactants thin out.

quiz.prompt: Are reaction orders determined from the balanced equation?
quiz.answer: No — they are determined experimentally and reflect the mechanism, not the stoichiometric coefficients.

quiz.prompt: A reaction is first order in A. If [A] doubles, what happens to the rate?
quiz.answer: The rate doubles, since rate ∝ [A]¹.

atoms.title: Activation energy and the Arrhenius equation
atoms.summary: The rate constant grows exponentially with temperature as more molecules clear the activation-energy barrier.

depths.eli5: Even a reaction that's 'downhill' overall often needs a running start — a hill it must get over before it can roll down the other side. That hill is why a log doesn't burst into flame on its own but does once you light a match. Heating the molecules gives them more energy, so many more of them can clear the hill, and the reaction speeds up dramatically.
depths.core: Most reactions have an energy hill called the activation energy, E_a — the minimum energy reactants must gather to reach the high-energy 'transition state' at the top, after which they tumble into products. The Arrhenius equation, k = A·e^(−E_a/RT), gives the rate constant k as a frequency factor A multiplied by e^(−E_a/RT), which is the fraction of molecules that have at least E_a worth of energy at temperature T (R is the gas constant). Because that fraction sits in an exponential, even a small rise in temperature can boost the rate enormously.
depths.deep: The exponential term is the 'Boltzmann tail' from kinetic theory — the small fraction of molecular collisions energetic enough to react. Taking the logarithm shows that plotting ln k against 1/T gives a straight line of slope −E_a/R, which is the standard experimental way to measure an activation energy. The factor A also folds in the geometric requirement that colliding molecules be lined up correctly to react.

quiz.prompt: What does the activation energy represent?
quiz.answer: The minimum energy barrier reactants must overcome (the transition state) for a reaction to occur.

quiz.prompt: How can you extract E_a from rate-constant measurements at several temperatures?
quiz.answer: Plot ln k versus 1/T; the slope is −E_a/R, so E_a = −R × slope.

atoms.title: Catalysis
atoms.summary: A catalyst speeds a reaction by providing a lower-energy pathway without being consumed.

depths.eli5: A catalyst is a helper that makes a reaction go faster without being used up itself. Picture it opening a shortcut over a smaller hill instead of the big one. Because the catalyst comes out of the reaction unchanged, the same little bit can help over and over. The catalytic converter in a car and the enzymes in your body all work this way.
depths.core: A catalyst speeds up a reaction by providing an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy (a smaller energy hill to climb). It speeds the forward and reverse reactions equally, and it is regenerated rather than consumed — so a tiny amount can process huge quantities of starting material (substrate). There are three flavors: homogeneous catalysis (catalyst in the same phase as the reactants, e.g. all dissolved in liquid), heterogeneous catalysis (a solid catalyst with reactants flowing over its surface), and enzymatic catalysis (biological catalysts — enzymes — in living things).
depths.deep: Because a catalyst lowers the activation energy for the forward and reverse directions by the same amount, it never changes the reaction's ΔG (the overall energy change) or where the equilibrium sits — it only shortens the time to reach equilibrium. Heterogeneous catalysts work by grabbing (adsorbing) reactant molecules onto their surface and weakening their bonds. Enzymes achieve their staggering speed-ups by precisely stabilizing the transition state, the fragile high-energy arrangement at the top of the hill.

quiz.prompt: How does a catalyst increase reaction rate?
quiz.answer: By providing an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy; it is not consumed.

quiz.prompt: Why does a catalyst not change the equilibrium position of a reaction?
quiz.answer: It lowers the activation energy for forward and reverse reactions equally, speeding both, so K and ΔG are unchanged — only the time to reach equilibrium is shorter.

atoms.title: Oxidation–reduction reactions
atoms.summary: Redox reactions transfer electrons, with one species oxidized (losing electrons) and another reduced (gaining them).

depths.eli5: A whole family of reactions is really about electrons being passed from one atom to another. The atom that gives electrons away is 'oxidized'; the atom that takes them is 'reduced'. You can never have one without the other — every giver needs a taker. Rusting, burning, and the reactions in a battery are all electron-passing reactions.
depths.core: A redox reaction (short for reduction–oxidation) is one in which electrons transfer from one species to another. Oxidation is the loss of electrons (and a rise in 'oxidation state'); reduction is the gain of electrons. They always happen together: whatever is oxidized hands its electrons to whatever is reduced. A handy memory aid is 'OIL RIG' — Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain. Chemists track which atom loses and which gains by assigning oxidation numbers, and they split the process into two half-reactions to balance the electrons cleanly. Redox underlies combustion (burning), corrosion (rusting), respiration (how your cells get energy), and batteries.
depths.deep: Balancing a redox reaction means conserving both atoms and electric charge; in acidic or basic water solutions you also balance using H⁺, OH⁻, and H₂O. Oxidation state is a formal bookkeeping device — you imagine giving every bond's shared electrons entirely to the more electronegative atom — so it isn't a real, physical charge, but it reliably tracks how electrons flow across a reaction.

atoms.art_prompt: electrons flowing from an oxidized atom to a reduced atom, with oxidation states changing labeled above each

quiz.prompt: What happens to a species that is oxidized?
quiz.answer: It loses electrons and its oxidation state increases.

quiz.prompt: In Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu, which species is oxidized?
quiz.answer: Zinc — it goes from 0 to +2, losing two electrons; Cu²⁺ is reduced to Cu.

atoms.title: Electrochemical cells
atoms.summary: Separating the half-reactions of a redox process lets electron flow do electrical work, linking cell voltage to free energy.

depths.eli5: In a redox reaction electrons jump from one atom to another. Here's the clever trick behind every battery: separate the electron-giver and the electron-taker into two compartments and connect them only by a wire. Now the electrons have to travel through the wire to get across — and electrons moving through a wire is electricity. You've built a battery.
depths.core: An electrochemical cell harnesses a redox reaction to make (or use) electricity. In a galvanic cell (a battery), oxidation and reduction are physically separated: oxidation happens at the anode, reduction at the cathode. Electrons released at the anode are forced through an external wire to the cathode, and that flow is the current; the push driving it is the voltage, called the cell potential. The standard cell potential E° is calculated from tabulated 'standard reduction potentials' for each half-reaction. The bridge to thermodynamics is ΔG° = −nFE°: here n is the number of electrons transferred and F is Faraday's constant. A positive E° gives a negative ΔG°, meaning the cell reaction is spontaneous and releases energy.
depths.deep: Faraday's constant F = 96,485 coulombs per mole of electrons — the electric charge carried by one mole of electrons. An electrolytic cell runs the same machinery in reverse: you apply an external voltage to force a nonspontaneous reaction (E° < 0) to happen, which is how metals are electroplated and aluminum is refined. A salt bridge connects the two compartments and lets ions flow to keep each side electrically neutral, so the current can keep going.

atoms.note: F = 96,485 C·mol⁻¹; n = moles of electrons transferred per reaction.
atoms.art_prompt: a galvanic cell: two beakers with electrodes, a wire carrying electrons, a salt bridge, voltmeter reading E°

quiz.prompt: At which electrode does oxidation occur?
quiz.answer: The anode.

quiz.prompt: Relate cell potential to spontaneity using ΔG° = −nFE°.
quiz.answer: A positive E° gives a negative ΔG° (since n and F are positive), so the cell reaction is spontaneous and releases energy.

atoms.title: The Nernst equation
atoms.summary: Cell potential under non-standard conditions depends on the reaction quotient through the Nernst equation.

depths.eli5: A battery's voltage isn't a fixed number — it slowly sags as the chemicals inside get used up, which is why an old battery is weaker. The Nernst equation is the formula that tells you exactly how the voltage depends on how much reactant is left. When everything is used up, the voltage hits zero: the battery is dead.
depths.core: The 'standard' cell potential E° assumes textbook conditions (every dissolved substance at 1 mol/L, every gas at 1 atmosphere). Real cells almost never run at those conditions. The Nernst equation, E = E° − (RT/nF)·ln Q, corrects the voltage for the actual amounts present, using the reaction quotient Q (the current ratio of products to reactants). As a battery discharges, products build up, Q rises toward the equilibrium constant K, and the voltage E falls toward zero. A 'dead' battery is simply one whose reaction has reached equilibrium, where there is no longer any push.
depths.deep: Setting E = 0 (equilibrium, Q = K) gives E° = (RT/nF) ln K, directly tying electrochemistry to the equilibrium constant. At 25 °C the messy prefactor RT/F simplifies, so with base-10 logarithms the term becomes 0.0592/n. The same equation underlies biological membrane potentials (the voltages nerve cells use to fire) and the pH electrode, where a difference in ion concentration is turned into a measurable voltage.

atoms.art_prompt: a cell-voltage curve declining as the reaction proceeds toward equilibrium, Q approaching K and E approaching 0

quiz.prompt: What is the cell potential when a battery reaches equilibrium?
quiz.answer: Zero — at equilibrium Q = K and E = 0, the battery is 'dead'.

quiz.prompt: Use the Nernst equation to relate E° to K.
quiz.answer: Set E = 0 at equilibrium where Q = K: 0 = E° − (RT/nF) ln K, so E° = (RT/nF) ln K.

atoms.title: Quantum chemistry: the Schrödinger picture of the atom
atoms.summary: Electronic structure is the set of solutions to the Schrödinger equation for electrons in the field of nuclei.

depths.eli5: All the dots, arrows, and orbital pictures in chemistry are really shortcuts for one deep equation from physics — a 'wave equation' that describes how electrons behave. Orbitals, chemical bonds, even the whole periodic table are just answers that fall out of solving it. In other words, chemistry is what quantum physics looks like when applied to electrons around atoms.
depths.core: Quantum chemistry treats electrons as waves governed by the Schrödinger equation, written Ĥψ = Eψ. In it, ψ (psi) is the wavefunction, a mathematical object that encodes where an electron is likely to be (its square, |ψ|², gives the probability of finding it at each point). Ĥ (the Hamiltonian) is the operator that represents the system's total energy, and E is an allowed energy value. The equation only permits certain solutions, which is why energies come in fixed, quantized levels. An orbital is simply a one-electron wavefunction. The shapes of orbitals, the lengths and strengths of bonds, and the lines in atomic spectra all emerge from solving — or approximating — this single equation.
depths.deep: Only the hydrogen atom (one electron) can be solved exactly. Every atom or molecule with more than one electron requires approximations, because the electrons repel each other and their motions become entangled — the 'electron correlation' problem. The Hartree–Fock method approximates this by treating each electron as moving in the averaged field of all the others. The entire field of computational chemistry exists to approximate Ĥψ = Eψ for molecules far too complex to solve by hand.

atoms.art_prompt: a hydrogen wavefunction probability cloud beside the equation Ĥψ=Eψ, with energy levels branching off

quiz.prompt: What does the wavefunction ψ describe?
quiz.answer: The quantum state of the electrons; |ψ|² gives the probability density of finding an electron at a location.

quiz.prompt: Why can't most atoms be solved exactly with the Schrödinger equation?
quiz.answer: Electron–electron repulsion couples the electrons' motions (the correlation problem), so only one-electron systems like hydrogen are exactly solvable; others need approximations.

atoms.title: Organic functional groups
atoms.summary: Carbon's versatility lets recurring atom groupings define families of molecules with predictable reactivity.

depths.eli5: Organic chemistry is the chemistry of carbon-based molecules — the stuff of life and most materials. It sounds overwhelming because there are millions of these molecules, but there's a shortcut: most of them are just a carbon skeleton with a few recurring 'gadgets' bolted on. Each gadget behaves the same way no matter what skeleton it's attached to, so once you know the gadgets, you can predict a lot.
depths.core: Carbon is special: it forms four strong covalent bonds and can link into chains and rings of any size, which is why there are so many carbon (organic) compounds. The key to organizing them is the functional group — a specific small cluster of atoms that gives a molecule its characteristic chemistry. Common examples: the alcohol group (–OH), the carbonyl group (a carbon double-bonded to oxygen, C=O, found in aldehydes and ketones), the carboxylic acid group (–COOH), and the amine group (–NH₂). A functional group concentrates the reactivity, so any molecule carrying that group behaves similarly regardless of the rest of its structure.
depths.deep: A functional group's behavior follows from its local bonding and polarity. For instance, the carbonyl carbon is electrophilic (electron-poor and so attractive to electron-rich species) because the oxygen pulls electron density away from it, making it a magnet for nucleophiles (electron-rich attackers). This modular picture — a fairly unreactive hydrocarbon skeleton decorated with reactive groups — is exactly what makes the enormous space of organic molecules learnable rather than hopeless.

atoms.art_prompt: a chart of common functional groups (–OH, C=O, –COOH, –NH₂) each on a generic carbon skeleton, labeled

quiz.prompt: What functional group defines a carboxylic acid?
quiz.answer: The carboxyl group, –COOH (a carbonyl bonded to a hydroxyl).

quiz.prompt: Why is the carbonyl carbon attractive to nucleophiles?
quiz.answer: Oxygen's electronegativity pulls electron density from the carbon, leaving it electrophilic (partially positive).

atoms.title: Isomerism
atoms.summary: Molecules with the same formula can differ in connectivity or spatial arrangement, changing their properties.

depths.eli5: Give two builders the exact same set of LEGO bricks and they might build completely different things. Molecules are the same way: two can have the identical count of each atom yet be totally different substances, just because the atoms are connected or arranged in space differently. Such molecules are called isomers.
depths.core: Isomers are molecules with the same molecular formula (the same atoms in the same numbers) but a different structure. There are two big families. Structural (constitutional) isomers differ in how the atoms are connected — the same parts wired together in a different order. Stereoisomers have the same connectivity but differ in their 3-D arrangement; these include cis/trans isomers (groups on the same vs. opposite sides of a rigid double bond) and enantiomers (a molecule and its non-superimposable mirror image, like your left and right hands). Even a subtle stereochemical difference can dramatically change how a molecule behaves in the body.
depths.deep: A common source of handedness (chirality) is a carbon atom bonded to four different groups. The two mirror-image forms (enantiomers) have identical ordinary physical properties and differ only in two ways: they rotate polarized light in opposite directions, and they interact differently with other handed molecules. That second point is why one enantiomer of a drug can be a cure while its mirror image is useless or even harmful — and it connects directly to a deep puzzle in biophysics, homochirality (why life uses only one handedness of its key molecules).
