quiz.prompt: What is the difference between structural isomers and stereoisomers?
quiz.answer: Structural isomers differ in atom connectivity; stereoisomers share connectivity but differ in spatial arrangement.

quiz.prompt: What structural feature makes a carbon atom a chirality center?
quiz.answer: Being bonded to four different groups, which makes the molecule non-superimposable on its mirror image.

atoms.title: Organic reaction types
atoms.summary: Most organic transformations sort into a few mechanistic classes driven by electron-pair movement.

depths.eli5: There are millions of known organic reactions, but they mostly follow just a few basic recipes: swap one group for another, add a new piece across a double bond, pull a piece off, or shuffle the atoms around. And underneath all of them is one idea — electrons moving from places that are electron-rich to places that are electron-poor.
depths.core: Most organic reactions fall into four broad classes: substitution (one group replaces another), addition (atoms add across a double or triple bond), elimination (a small piece is removed, often creating a double bond), and rearrangement (atoms reshuffle within the molecule) — frequently combined with oxidation or reduction. The common engine driving them is the nucleophile–electrophile interaction: an electron-rich site (the nucleophile) attacks an electron-poor site (the electrophile). Chemists trace these moves with 'curved arrows', each showing where a pair of electrons goes. Recognizing which class a reaction belongs to lets you predict its products and the conditions it needs.
depths.deep: The organizing principle is the mechanism — the actual step-by-step path — not just the final product. For example, the two substitution mechanisms SN1 and SN2 differ in whether the old bond breaks before or at the same time as the new bond forms, which in turn controls the reaction's stereochemistry (3-D outcome) and how its rate depends on concentration. Whole networks of such elementary steps, now increasingly mapped by computer, are how chemists design complex syntheses and understand the metabolic pathways inside cells.

atoms.art_prompt: curved-arrow mechanism of a nucleophile attacking an electrophilic carbon, leaving group departing

quiz.prompt: Name the four broad classes of organic reactions.
quiz.answer: Substitution, addition, elimination, and rearrangement (often with oxidation/reduction).

quiz.prompt: Explain the general nucleophile–electrophile picture of organic reactivity.
quiz.answer: Electron-rich nucleophiles donate an electron pair to electron-poor electrophilic sites, forming new bonds; curved arrows trace these electron-pair movements through the mechanism.

atoms.title: Thermodynamic vs kinetic control
atoms.summary: Whether a reaction yields the most stable product or the fastest-formed one depends on conditions.

depths.eli5: When a reaction could make more than one product, two different questions matter. Which product forms fastest? And which product is the most stable once formed? They aren't always the same molecule. Give the reaction little time and low heat and you tend to get the fast one; give it lots of time and heat and the most stable one eventually wins out.
depths.core: Two separate ideas govern which product you get. Thermodynamics (measured by Gibbs free energy, ΔG) tells you which product is most stable. Kinetics (measured by activation energy, E_a) tells you which product forms fastest — the one with the smallest energy barrier. When two products compete: low temperature and short reaction times favor the kinetic product (the quick-to-form one), while high temperature and long times let the system find its way to the thermodynamic product (the most stable one). These need not be the same molecule, so the conditions you choose decide the outcome.
depths.deep: This distinction is the practical heart of designing a synthesis, because it determines selectivity (which product you actually get). For thermodynamic control to win, the kinetic product must be able to revert — the reaction has to be reversible — so the system can back out and find the more stable option. The same logic explains why diamond persists at room temperature even though graphite is the more stable form of carbon: the barrier to convert diamond into graphite is astronomically high, so kinetics traps it indefinitely.

quiz.prompt: What conditions favor the thermodynamic product over the kinetic one?
quiz.answer: Higher temperature and longer reaction times (allowing the system to reach the most stable product).

quiz.prompt: Why does diamond persist at room temperature even though graphite is more stable?
quiz.answer: The activation barrier to convert diamond to graphite is enormous, so the reaction is kinetically trapped despite being thermodynamically favorable.

atoms.title: Computational chemistry and reaction networks
atoms.summary: Approximate solutions of the electronic Schrödinger equation let computers predict structures, energies, and reaction pathways.

depths.eli5: Running real chemistry experiments is slow and expensive. So chemists let computers do the quantum math (approximately) to predict how a molecule will look and how it will react — before anyone touches a test tube. Lately, computers can even map whole webs of possible reactions automatically, suggesting routes a human might never think of.
depths.core: Computational chemistry uses computers to approximate the electronic Schrödinger equation and predict a molecule's geometry (its shape), energies, and reactivity. Solving that equation exactly is impossible for real molecules, so methods make trade-offs. A widely used one is density functional theory (DFT), which cleverly works with the electron density (how electrons are spread out in space) instead of the full, far more complex wavefunction — this makes medium-sized molecules practical to compute. Linking many elementary reaction steps together produces a 'reaction network': a searchable map of intermediates and transition states that turns planning a synthesis into a graph-search problem.
depths.deep: Every method balances accuracy against computational cost. Hartree–Fock ignores electron correlation (the way electrons' motions are interdependent); 'post-Hartree–Fock' methods add it back but become very expensive; DFT approximates it through an 'exchange-correlation functional'. The current frontier — machine-learned interatomic potentials and automated transition-state searches — aims to explore enormous reaction networks at near-quantum accuracy for a fraction of the cost, closing the loop back to the foundational equation Ĥψ = Eψ.

atoms.note: This is the live frontier: ML potentials and automated reaction-network discovery are reshaping how chemistry is predicted rather than only measured.
atoms.art_prompt: a reaction-network graph of intermediates and transition states with computed energies, a DFT electron-density isosurface beside it

quiz.prompt: What quantity does density functional theory use instead of the full wavefunction?
quiz.answer: The electron density.

quiz.prompt: Explain why computational chemistry methods involve a trade-off between accuracy and cost.
quiz.answer: Capturing electron correlation precisely (post-Hartree–Fock) is computationally expensive; cheaper methods like DFT approximate it, so chemists choose the level that balances acceptable accuracy against feasible computation for the molecule's size.

atoms.title: Coordination complexes and crystal field theory
atoms.summary: Transition-metal ions bind surrounding ligands, and the resulting d-orbital splitting explains color and magnetism.

depths.eli5: Picture a metal ion sitting in the middle, with several molecules clamped around it like the fingers of a claw. This claw-like grip subtly bends the energy levels of the metal's electrons — and that bending is why these compounds come in such vivid colors. The deep blue of many copper solutions and the red of blood both come from arrangements like this.
depths.core: A coordination complex is a central metal ion surrounded by molecules or ions called ligands that bond to it by donating a pair of electrons (ligands act as Lewis bases — electron-pair donors). Crystal field theory explains the consequences: the ligands' electric field pushes on the metal's five d orbitals and splits them into groups of different energy. The size of that energy gap controls two things. First, the complex's color — the complex absorbs light whose energy matches the gap, and you see the leftover colors. Second, how the d electrons arrange: they can pair up tightly in the lower group (low spin) or spread out into the higher group (high spin).
depths.deep: The crystal-field splitting, written Δ, depends on the complex's geometry (octahedral, tetrahedral, etc.) and on how strongly the ligands push, ranked by the 'spectrochemical series'. If Δ is larger than the energy cost of pairing two electrons, electrons pair in the lower set (low spin); if smaller, they occupy the upper set unpaired (high spin) — and the number of unpaired electrons sets the complex's magnetism. A refinement called ligand-field theory blends this with molecular-orbital ideas, and it is central to bioinorganic chemistry, such as the iron at the heart of hemoglobin that carries oxygen in your blood.

quiz.answer: They split into sets of different energy (e.g., t2g and eg in octahedral geometry), separated by the crystal-field splitting Δ.

quiz.answer: Whether the splitting Δ is smaller than the electron-pairing energy (high spin) or larger (low spin), set by ligand strength and geometry.

atoms.title: Bond energy and reaction enthalpy from bonds
atoms.summary: Reaction enthalpy can be estimated as the energy to break reactant bonds minus the energy released forming product bonds.

depths.eli5: Pulling a chemical bond apart takes energy, like stretching a spring until it snaps. Forming a new bond gives energy back. So whether a reaction warms up or cools down is just a tug-of-war: the energy you spend breaking the old bonds versus the energy you get back making the new ones.
depths.core: Every type of bond has a characteristic strength, called its average bond-dissociation energy — the energy needed to break it. Breaking bonds always absorbs energy (endothermic); forming bonds always releases energy (exothermic). So a reaction's overall heat can be estimated as ΔH_rxn ≈ (sum of energies of bonds broken) − (sum of energies of bonds formed). This gives a quick prediction of whether a reaction gives off or takes in heat, and it links molecular structure directly to the energetics (thermochemistry) of a reaction.
depths.deep: Bond energies are averages taken over many different molecules, so this method is only approximate; using Hess's law with tabulated formation enthalpies is more accurate. Even so, the bond-energy view explains a lot: combustion releases so much heat because very strong C=O and O–H bonds form in the products, and high-energy compounds (like many nitrogen explosives) release enormous energy when they rearrange into the extraordinarily stable triple bond of nitrogen gas (N₂).

quiz.answer: Endothermic — energy must be supplied to break a bond.

atoms.title: Titration and equivalence
atoms.summary: Adding a known reagent until stoichiometric equivalence lets you measure an unknown concentration.

depths.eli5: Suppose you have some acid but don't know how concentrated it is. Here's a clever way to find out: slowly drip in a base whose strength you do know, until it has exactly cancelled all the acid. The amount of base it took tells you precisely how much acid was there. This drip-and-measure technique is called a titration.
depths.core: A titration measures an unknown concentration by reacting it with a solution you know exactly. You slowly add the standardized titrant (the known solution) to the analyte (the unknown) until you reach the equivalence point — the moment when the moles of added reagent exactly match the analyte according to the reaction's stoichiometry. For an acid–base titration, a plot of pH versus volume added shows a sharp jump right at equivalence; a color-changing indicator or a pH meter signals when you're there. Knowing the volume and concentration of titrant used, you calculate the unknown concentration directly.
depths.deep: The equivalence point isn't always at pH 7. When a weak acid is titrated with a strong base, the equivalence point is basic (above 7), because the product left behind is the acid's conjugate base, which is itself slightly basic. There's a bonus: at the half-equivalence point (halfway to equivalence) the solution is an equal-parts buffer, so pH = pK_a there. That means a single titration curve gives you both the unknown's concentration and the acid's strength (pK_a) at once.

quiz.prompt: What is the equivalence point of a titration?
quiz.answer: The point where the moles of added titrant exactly match the analyte according to the reaction stoichiometry.

quiz.prompt: Why is the equivalence point of a weak acid titrated with strong base above pH 7?
quiz.answer: The product is the conjugate base of the weak acid, which is basic in solution, raising the pH above 7.

atoms.title: Oxidation states
atoms.summary: A bookkeeping charge assigned by giving shared electrons to the more electronegative atom tracks electron flow.

depths.eli5: Here's a handy bookkeeping trick. For every bond, pretend the shared electrons belong entirely to the greedier (more electronegative) atom. Then count up whether each atom ended up with more or fewer electrons than it normally has. That count, written as a + or − number, is the atom's oxidation state. It's not the atom's real charge — it's a tally that helps you track where electrons go.
depths.core: An oxidation state (or oxidation number) is the hypothetical charge an atom would carry if every one of its bonds were treated as fully ionic, with the shared electrons handed to the more electronegative partner. A few simple rules let you assign them fast: a pure element is 0, oxygen is usually −2, hydrogen is usually +1, and all the oxidation states in a species must add up to its overall charge. Oxidation states are the main tool for spotting redox reactions (where the numbers change) and for balancing them, since a rise means electrons lost and a fall means electrons gained.
depths.deep: Oxidation state is a formal accounting device, not a physical measurement — the actual partial charge on an atom is usually much smaller and not a whole number. Its real value comes from conservation: the total increase in oxidation states must exactly equal the total decrease, because every electron lost by one atom is gained by another. That balance is precisely what makes redox equation-balancing and electrochemical calculations work.

atoms.title: Vapor pressure and the Clausius–Clapeyron relation
atoms.summary: The vapor pressure of a liquid rises exponentially with temperature, governed by its enthalpy of vaporization.

depths.eli5: Leave a glass of water out and some of it slowly turns to vapor and drifts away — that's evaporation. Warm the water and it evaporates much faster: its 'urge' to become vapor climbs steeply as it heats up. This urge is called vapor pressure, and a single equation captures how fast it rises with temperature.
depths.core: In a closed container, a liquid keeps evaporating and condensing until those two rates balance; the pressure of vapor sitting above the liquid at that balance is the vapor pressure. The Clausius–Clapeyron relation describes how vapor pressure climbs — exponentially — as temperature rises, governed by the liquid's enthalpy of vaporization, ΔH_vap (the energy needed to turn it into vapor). A liquid boils when its vapor pressure rises to equal the surrounding air pressure. That's why water boils at a lower temperature high on a mountain, where the air pressure is lower — and why food takes longer to cook up there.
depths.deep: The relation is derived by setting the molar Gibbs energies of the liquid and the vapor equal along their coexistence line and treating the vapor as an ideal gas. A plot of ln P against 1/T comes out as a straight line with slope −ΔH_vap/R, the standard way to measure vaporization enthalpies. Notice it has the same mathematical shape as the Arrhenius equation (kinetics) and the van't Hoff equation (equilibrium) — all three trace back to the same underlying Boltzmann statistics of energy.

quiz.prompt: What molecular quantity governs how steeply vapor pressure rises with temperature?
quiz.answer: The enthalpy of vaporization, ΔH_vap.

quiz.prompt: Why does water boil at a lower temperature at high altitude?
quiz.answer: Atmospheric pressure is lower, so the vapor pressure equals the external pressure (boiling condition) at a lower temperature.

atoms.title: Reaction mechanisms and elementary steps
atoms.summary: An overall reaction is a sequence of elementary steps, the slowest of which sets the observed rate.

depths.eli5: A reaction written on paper as 'A turns into B' usually doesn't happen in one big leap. Behind the scenes it's a series of small molecular moves, one after another. And just like a checkout line, the slowest single move is the bottleneck — it sets how fast the whole reaction can go, no matter how quick the other steps are.
depths.core: A reaction mechanism is the detailed, step-by-step molecular path from reactants to products. It is built from elementary steps — single molecular events that actually occur, classified by how many molecules collide in them (one = unimolecular, two = bimolecular). The slowest elementary step is the rate-determining step, and it controls the overall rate law. This is why a reaction's experimentally measured order often doesn't match the coefficients in the overall balanced equation. Along the way, short-lived intermediates are produced and then used up. A proposed mechanism is only valid if it reproduces the rate law actually observed in experiments.
depths.deep: For an elementary step — and only an elementary step — the molecularity (how many molecules are involved) does equal the order in its rate law; this is the special case where you can read the rate law straight from the equation. To predict the overall rate law of a multi-step mechanism, chemists use approximations like the steady-state approximation (intermediate concentration stays roughly constant) or the pre-equilibrium approximation, then check the prediction against experiment.

quiz.prompt: Which step in a mechanism determines the overall reaction rate?
quiz.answer: The rate-determining step — the slowest elementary step.

quiz.prompt: Why can the order of an overall reaction differ from its stoichiometric coefficients?
quiz.answer: The rate law reflects the mechanism's rate-determining step, not the overall balanced equation; only elementary steps have orders equal to their molecularity.

atoms.title: Linking equilibrium constant to free energy
atoms.summary: The equilibrium constant is the exponential of the standard free-energy change, unifying thermodynamics and equilibrium.

depths.eli5: Two ideas you've met separately turn out to be the same fact in disguise. How far a reaction goes before settling (its equilibrium constant K) and how 'downhill' the reaction is (its free-energy change ΔG°) are tied together by one equation — one is essentially the logarithm of the other. So if you know how downhill a reaction is, you already know how far it will go, without running it.
depths.core: The standard free-energy change ΔG° and the equilibrium constant K are two faces of the same thermodynamics, linked by ΔG° = −RT ln K (R is the gas constant, T the absolute temperature, ln the natural logarithm). A negative ΔG° (a favorable, downhill reaction) makes K greater than 1, meaning equilibrium favors products; a positive ΔG° makes K less than 1, favoring reactants; ΔG° = 0 gives K = 1. This single relation lets you predict where a reaction's equilibrium will sit using only tabulated thermodynamic data — no experiment required.
depths.deep: Combine this with ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS° and you get the van't Hoff equation, which shows how K changes with temperature: ln K shifts by −ΔH°/RT, so an endothermic reaction's K rises as you heat it while an exothermic reaction's K falls. This is the quantitative engine behind Le Chatelier's temperature predictions, and it connects onward to electrochemistry through E° = (RT/nF) ln K.

quiz.prompt: What is the relationship between ΔG° and K?
quiz.answer: ΔG° = −RT ln K.

quiz.prompt: If ΔG° = 0, what is the value of K?
quiz.answer: K = 1, since 0 = −RT ln K requires ln K = 0.

atoms.title: Colligative properties
atoms.summary: Dissolved particles lower vapor pressure and freezing point and raise boiling point, depending only on how many they are.

depths.eli5: Dissolve something into a liquid and you change when it freezes and boils: salty water freezes below 0 °C and boils above 100 °C. Here's the surprising part — what matters is how many dissolved particles there are, not what kind they are. This is why we throw salt on icy roads and put antifreeze in car engines.
depths.core: Colligative properties are the handful of solution behaviors that depend only on the number of dissolved solute particles, not their chemical identity. The four are: vapor-pressure lowering (the liquid evaporates less readily), boiling-point elevation (it boils at a higher temperature), freezing-point depression (it freezes at a lower temperature), and osmotic pressure (the pressure that drives solvent across a membrane into the solution). Adding any solute lowers the solvent's vapor pressure and shifts where it freezes and boils — which is exactly why salt melts ice on roads and antifreeze keeps an engine's coolant liquid across a wider temperature range.
depths.deep: The underlying cause is entropy: dissolved particles raise the disorder of the liquid, making the liquid state more stable relative to the pure-solvent solid and vapor, which pushes the freezing point down and the boiling point up. Osmotic pressure (given by Π = MRT, the van't Hoff form, where M is molarity) can become surprisingly large; it underlies the turgor that keeps plant cells firm and the reverse-osmosis process used to desalinate seawater — a direct bridge from chemistry into biophysics.

quiz.prompt: What do colligative properties depend on?
quiz.answer: The number (concentration) of dissolved solute particles, not their identity.

quiz.prompt: Why does salt lower the freezing point of water?
quiz.answer: Dissolved ions raise the liquid's entropy, stabilizing it relative to ice, so a lower temperature is needed to freeze it (freezing-point depression).
